blocks.text: The genitive answers *kogo? czego?*, “of whom? of what?” It is the most frequent case in the lessons after the nominative, because its uses go well beyond “of”: it follows quantities and the numbers from five up, replaces the accusative after negation, expresses absence, and is required by many prepositions and verbs.
Endings: singular

examples
rows: *pana, Tomasza, Krakowa, Gdańska, szampana* · *czasu, Rynku, Wawelu, roku, szacunku*
*-y*; *-i* after k, g and soft stems (incl. *-ja*, *-ia*)
*siostry, Kanady, mowy, pracy* · *fonetyki, Woli, komisji, babci, nadziei*

blocks.text: Masculine nouns ending in *-a* (*kolega*, *mężczyzna*) take the feminine ending: *kolegi*.
Masculine -a or -u?
This is the one part of the genitive that has to be learned word by word. There are tendencies, though:

head: usually -a
usually -u
rows: many place names that aren’t towns: *Wawelu, Rynku*

blocks.text: Exceptions are common enough (*chleba*, *szampana*, *tygodnia*, *komputera*) that a dictionary entry always gives the genitive. Learn it with the noun: *rok, roku*; *chleb, chleba*.
Endings: plural

head: ending
examples
rows: fem. nouns in *-ość*, *-ść* and soft consonants

blocks.text: When the ending disappears, the stem often adjusts. An *e* is inserted to break up a consonant cluster (*jabłko → jabłek*, *kanapka → kanapek*), and a vowel in the now-closed syllable may change (*święta → świąt*, *droga → dróg*). A few nouns are irregular: *rok → lat*, *dziecko → dzieci*, *człowiek → ludzi*.
Use 1: “of”
The second of two nouns is genitive when it describes or owns the first:
Use 2: quantities and numbers

Words for amounts and containers take the genitive (*kilo ziemniaków*, *butelka wina*, *dużo czasu*, *trochę cukru*, *ile jabłek?*), and so do the numbers from five upward (*pięć jabłek*, *dwanaście złotych*, *dziesięć sztuk*). With two to four, the noun stays in the ordinary plural: *dwa rodzaje*, *trzy złote*.
With perfective verbs of eating, drinking and giving, the genitive can mean “some”: *Napijesz się kawy?*, “Will you have some coffee?”; compare *Wypiłem kawę*, “I drank the coffee.”
Use 3: negation
A direct object in the accusative switches to the genitive when the verb is negated:
Only accusative objects change. Objects in other cases stay as they are: *Pomagam mu* → *Nie pomagam mu* (dative); *Interesuję się sportem* → *Nie interesuję się sportem* (instrumental).
Use 4: absence
“There is no …” is *nie ma* + genitive, in every tense. The verb is impersonal and never agrees with the noun:
Use 5: prepositions

head: preposition
meaning
examples
rows: *do Rynku, do rodziców, do Kanady, do poniedziałku*
*z Gdańska, z pracy*; also a subject of study: *doktorat z fonetyki*
*od rodziców, od jutra, od dwudziestu lat*

blocks.text: Watch *z*: with the genitive it means “from” (*z Gdańska*), with the instrumental “with” (*z przyjemnością*). And *do* with a person means “to their place”: *jadę do rodziców*, “I’m going to my parents’.”
Use 6: verbs that take the genitive
A number of common verbs take a genitive object instead of an accusative:
Wishes and greetings

Because *życzyć* takes the genitive, wishes stay genitive even when the verb is dropped: *(Życzę) Wesołych Świąt!*, *Szczęśliwego Nowego Roku!*, *Miłego dnia!*, *Smacznego!*, *Wszystkiego najlepszego!* The same is true of a list of wishes: *zdrowia, szczęścia, spełnienia marzeń*.
Dates
Saying “on” a date uses the genitive of the ordinal and the month: *dwudziestego czwartego grudnia*, “on 24 December”; *pierwszego stycznia*, “on 1 January.”
